etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin collidere (“to strike or clash together”), from com- (“together”) + laedere (“to strike, dash against, hurt”); see lesion.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To impact directly, especially if violent.

quote.citation: 1865, John Tyndall, The Constitution of the Universe, published 1869, page 14:
quote.text: Across this space the attraction urges them. They collide, they recoil, they oscillate.

quote.citation: 1837, Thomas Carlyle, The French Revolution: A History […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London: Chapman and Hall, →OCLC, (please specify the book or page number):
quote.text: No longer rocking and swaying, but clashing and colliding.

quote.citation: 2012 June 2, Phil McNulty, “England 1-0 Belgium”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: And this friendly was not without its injury worries, with defender Gary Cahill substituted early on after a nasty, needless push by Dries Mertens that caused him to collide with goalkeeper Joe Hart, an incident that left the Chelsea defender requiring a precautionary X-ray at Wembley.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To come into conflict, or be incompatible.
(poetic, intransitive) To meet; to come into contact.

quote.citation: 2004, “Collide”, in Stop All the World Now, performed by Howie Day:
quote.text: Out of the doubts that fill my mind / I somehow find, you and I collide

quote.citation: 2009, “Hey, Soul Sister”, in Save Me, San Francisco, performed by Train:
quote.text: I knew when we collided / you're the one I have decided who's one of my kind
